thesis_claim: Financial ratios and accounting fundamentals are valid early-warning inputs, but not a novel idea by themselves.
Firm-period and forward-looking target design are better aligned with early warning than one static firm observation.
Strict legal bankruptcy/distress is rare and should be treated as a benchmark, not the whole success/failure story.
A broader financial-pressure target is defensible when it is clearly separated from legal bankruptcy.
ML models are defensible for distress prediction only when benchmarked and temporally validated.

thesis_claim: PR-AUC and positive-class recall/F1 must be shown for rare or imbalanced targets.
Feature importance and SHAP-style explanations describe model behavior, not economic causality.
Missing values in accounting panels must not be silently converted into zeros or invented persistence.
Macro/credit variables are useful context, but claims that macro dominates firm fundamentals require empirical evidence.
The artifact can be justified as design science and decision support if it connects data, models, interpretation, and user exploration.
Strategic success/resilience framing is acceptable only if the operational financial proxy is explicit.
supporting_citation_keys: barney1991firm; teece1997dynamic; hannan1984structural; duchek2020resilience; hepfer2022organizational; linnenluecke2017resilience

thesis_claim: Distress-prediction variables may not transfer cleanly across institutional settings; emerging-market and Russian evidence supports cautious interpretation of accounting, market, and macro predictors.

Russian bankruptcy-prediction literature suggests external macroeconomic factors and market context can improve or alter firm-failure analysis, but these sources support context/future extension rather than current U.S. model claims.
Russia and the United States should not be treated as interchangeable macro-financial environments; any cross-country extension requires separate data design and validation.
